title: The cluster: KRaft, replicas and the ISR
goal: By the end you can explain what the KRaft controllers do, how a leader, its followers, the ISR and the high watermark decide when a write is committed, and what `acks=all` and `min.insync.replicas` really guarantee.

warmup.q: A topic has replication factor 3 and the default `min.insync.replicas` of 1. Both followers fall out of sync. A producer sends with `acks=all`. What happens?
options: The write fails, because `acks=all` needs all three replicas
The write succeeds once the leader alone has it, because `acks=all` waits only for the replicas currently in sync
The write waits until both followers are back in sync
The broker quietly downgrades the producer to `acks=0`
warmup.why: `acks=all` means every replica in the current ISR, and the ISR has shrunk to the leader. With `min.insync.replicas=1` the leader alone is enough, so the producer is told the write is safe while one disk holds it. Setting `min.insync.replicas=2` makes the leader refuse such writes instead, which is what the first option expects to happen by default.

sections.h: One copy is one disk away from losing payments: replication
sections.body:
So far every partition has lived on one broker's disk. Lesson 1 of this track called it a log: records numbered by offset, appended at the end. Lesson 2 showed that on disk the log is a directory of segment files. Now the disk dies, or the broker's host reboots for a kernel patch. While it is down nobody can write `payments-0` or read it, and if the disk is gone, so are the payments in it.

The obvious fix is to keep copies of each partition on other brokers. The number of copies is the topic's **replication factor**; 3 is the usual choice for anything you care about. Each copy is called a **replica**.

How do the copies stay identical? Suppose producers wrote to all three replicas themselves. Two producers sending at the same moment could reach the replicas in different orders, and then offset 7 would be one payment on broker 1 and another payment on broker 2. The copies would disagree about the very thing lesson 1 promised: what each offset means.

So Kafka makes one replica the **leader**. Producers send every write to the leader, and only the leader assigns offsets. The other replicas are **followers**. Each follower sends fetch requests to the leader, the same kind of request a consumer sends, and appends what comes back to its own copy at the same offsets. Consumers read from the leader too.

Each replica has its own **log end offset** (LEO), the offset its next record will get. The leader's LEO moves first, and the followers' LEOs catch up a few milliseconds later as their fetches return. Every fetch request carries the follower's LEO, so the leader always knows how far each follower has got.

That raises the question of when a record is safe. If the leader told the producer "done" after writing only its own copy, and then died, the record would exist nowhere else. So the leader tracks the replicas that are keeping up with it, the **in-sync replicas** or **ISR**, and computes the **high watermark** (HW): the smallest LEO among the ISR. Every record below the HW is on every in-sync replica. Those records are **committed**. The leader is always in the ISR; the last section of this lesson shows how a follower leaves it.

The high watermark does two jobs. Consumers read only below it, so they never see a record that could vanish if the leader died. And it decides when a careful producer hears back. A producer chooses how long the leader should wait before replying with its `acks` setting: `acks=1` means "reply once your own copy has it", and `acks=all` means "reply once every in-sync replica has it", that is, once the HW has passed the record. `acks=all` is the default since Kafka 3.0.

Leaders are spread across brokers, so the write load is too. A topic with 3 partitions and replication factor 3 on three brokers gives each broker one partition to lead and two to follow. When the leader's broker fails, a follower that has every committed record takes over. A replica that missed committed records must never become leader, because the records it lacks would vanish without any error. Kafka calls that an **unclean leader election** and forbids it by default (`unclean.leader.election.enable=false`); the partition goes offline instead of losing data.

try.title: Start a three-node cluster and read a topic's layout
steps: From the `labs` folder, start the cluster: `docker compose -f env/kafka-cluster.yml up -d --wait`. It runs three Kafka nodes, needs about 2 GB of memory and is ready in about 10 seconds.
Create `payments` with 3 partitions, replication factor 3 and `min.insync.replicas=2` (explained in the last section), then describe it with the command below.
Read one line per partition: `Leader`, `Replicas`, `Isr`. Which broker leads each partition? Keep the cluster running for the next Try-its.

code.title: from the labs folder
code.src:
docker compose -f env/kafka-cluster.yml exec kafka-1 bash -c '
  cd /opt/kafka/bin
  ./kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server kafka-1:19092 --create --topic payments \
    --partitions 3 --replication-factor 3 --config min.insync.replicas=2
  ./kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server kafka-1:19092 --describe --topic payments'

try.expect:
```text
Created topic payments.
Topic: payments	TopicId: enir7IEoQIGQPA8K16pUhQ	PartitionCount: 3	ReplicationFactor: 3	Configs: min.insync.replicas=2
	Topic: payments	Partition: 0	Leader: 3	Replicas: 3,1,2	Isr: 3,1,2	Elr: 	LastKnownElr: 
	Topic: payments	Partition: 1	Leader: 1	Replicas: 1,2,3	Isr: 1,2,3	Elr: 	LastKnownElr: 
	Topic: payments	Partition: 2	Leader: 2	Replicas: 2,3,1	Isr: 2,3,1	Elr: 	LastKnownElr: 
```
Each broker leads one partition and follows the other two. The first broker in `Replicas` is the partition's preferred leader, and all three replicas are in every ISR. Which broker gets which partition is chosen at random when the topic is created, so your layout and `TopicId` will differ. `Elr` and `LastKnownElr` are empty; they belong to eligible leader replicas, explained in Go deeper.

sections.h: Someone has to decide who leads: KRaft controllers
sections.body:
When the broker that leads `payments-2` dies, one of its followers must take over. If each broker decided for itself, two followers could both declare themselves leader after a network hiccup. Both would accept writes and give offset 500 to two different payments. This is called split brain, and it is the failure every replicated system is built to avoid.

So one place must decide, and every broker must follow its decisions. That place is the **controller**. It holds the cluster's **metadata**: which brokers are alive, which topics and partitions exist, which broker leads each partition and which replicas are in its ISR. When a leader's broker dies, the controller picks a new leader from the ISR and tells every broker.

A single controller would be a new single point of failure, so Kafka runs several, usually three, and they must agree. They use **KRaft**, Kafka's own implementation of Raft, a protocol for keeping a log identical on several machines by majority vote. The controllers keep the metadata as a log, the internal topic `__cluster_metadata`, with one partition. Every change is a record in it: a topic created, a broker fenced, a new leader for `payments-2`. One controller is active, the Raft leader: it appends changes, and the other controllers replicate them. A change counts once a majority has it, two of three. That's why controller counts are odd: three controllers survive one failure, five survive two, and four still survive only one.

If the active controller dies, the others elect a new one within a couple of seconds (`controller.quorum.election.timeout.ms` is 1 second). Each election raises the **leader epoch**, a counter that lets every node ignore requests from a leader that has been replaced.

Brokers fetch the metadata log from the active controller and apply it, much like a consumer reads a topic. Each broker also sends the controller a heartbeat every 2 seconds (`broker.heartbeat.interval.ms`). If a broker misses heartbeats for 9 seconds (`broker.session.timeout.ms`), the controller **fences** it: it stops treating the broker as alive, removes it from every ISR and moves its leaderships to in-sync followers. A broker that shuts down cleanly tells the controller first, so the move happens at once.

A node can be a broker, a controller or both (`process.roles=broker,controller`, called combined mode). The lab cluster runs three combined nodes to save memory. Production clusters usually put the controllers on their own small machines, so that a busy broker can't slow down the metadata quorum and losing brokers never costs the controller majority.

Before Kafka 4.0, this metadata lived in a separate system, ZooKeeper. Kafka 3.9 was the last release that could use it; since 4.0, KRaft is the only mode.

try.title: Find the active controller, then stop it
steps: Run the first command. Note `LeaderId` and `LeaderEpoch`.

Stop the node whose id is the `LeaderId`. It was 2 in the run below; use yours. If it is 1, run the other commands on `kafka-2` instead (`exec kafka-2 ... --bootstrap-server kafka-2:19092`). Predict what happens to `LeaderEpoch`, then ask a node that is still up.
Start the stopped node again and look at every voter with `describe --replication`. Keep the cluster running.

code.title: from the labs folder
code.src:
# who leads the metadata quorum?
docker compose -f env/kafka-cluster.yml exec kafka-1 /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-metadata-quorum.sh \
  --bootstrap-server kafka-1:19092 describe --status

# stop the node with that LeaderId (2 in the run below), then ask a node that is still up
docker compose -f env/kafka-cluster.yml stop kafka-2
docker compose -f env/kafka-cluster.yml exec kafka-1 /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-metadata-quorum.sh \
  --bootstrap-server kafka-1:19092 describe --status

# bring it back and look at every voter
docker compose -f env/kafka-cluster.yml start kafka-2
sleep 8
docker compose -f env/kafka-cluster.yml exec kafka-1 /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-metadata-quorum.sh \
  --bootstrap-server kafka-1:19092 describe --replication

```text

1     	AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA	108         	0  	1794075635752     	1794075635752        	Leader
2     	AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA	108         	0  	1794075635515     	1794075635515        	Follower
3     	AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA	108         	0  	1794075635514     	1794075635514        	Follower
```
A new active controller took over within a couple of seconds, and the epoch went up. It jumped from 1 to 3 here and from 1 to 2 in another run: an election round that doesn't finish uses up an epoch too. Which node wins and the offsets will differ for you. `HighWatermark` belongs to the metadata log: the offset up to which a majority of controllers have the records. After the restart, node 2 has caught up and its lag is 0: the metadata log is replicated much like a partition.

sections.h: acks=all waits for the ISR, and min.insync.replicas sets the floor
sections.body:
A follower is alive but slow, because its disk has stalled. Should the leader wait for it before it tells producers a write is safe? If it always waits for every replica, one slow disk stalls every producer on the partition. If it never waits, a write the producer was told is safe can disappear with the leader.

Kafka's answer sits in between: the leader waits for the ISR, and drops followers that fall behind. A follower leaves the ISR in one of two ways. If its broker stops heartbeating, the controller fences the broker after 9 seconds and removes it from every ISR. If the broker is alive but the follower can't keep up, the leader removes it once it has not caught up to the leader's end for `replica.lag.time.max.ms`, 30 seconds by default. Fetching is not enough: the follower has to reach the end. When it catches up to the high watermark again, it rejoins.

While a slow follower is still in the ISR, it holds the high watermark back, and every `acks=all` producer waits with it. Once the leader removes it, the HW jumps forward and the waiting producers get their replies. Step through it below.

`acks=all` does not mean all replicas. It means all replicas **currently in the ISR**. If the ISR shrinks to the leader alone, one copy on one disk satisfies `acks=all`. The producer hears that the write is safe, and losing that one broker loses the write.

`min.insync.replicas` closes that gap. It is the smallest ISR size at which the leader accepts an `acks=all` write, and you set it on the topic:

```java
NewTopic payments = new NewTopic("payments", 3, (short) 3)          // 3 partitions, 3 replicas
        .configs(Map.of("min.insync.replicas", "2"));               // acks=all needs 2 in sync
admin.createTopics(List.of(payments)).all().get();
```

```kotlin
val payments = NewTopic("payments", 3, 3.toShort())                 // 3 partitions, 3 replicas
    .configs(mapOf("min.insync.replicas" to "2"))                   // acks=all needs 2 in sync
admin.createTopics(listOf(payments)).all().get()
```

With replication factor 3 and `min.insync.replicas=2`, you can lose one replica and keep writing, and every acknowledged write is on at least two brokers. If the ISR drops to one, the leader refuses `acks=all` writes with the error `NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS`. The default is 1, which guarantees nothing of the kind. The `KafkaProducer` javadoc recommends replication factor 3 with `min.insync.replicas=2` for transactional topics, and it is the right setting for payments too.

Two details catch people. `min.insync.replicas` applies only to `acks=all`, so an `acks=1` producer, which waits for the leader alone, writes straight past the floor. And `NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS` is a retriable error. Your send doesn't fail at once: the producer logs a warning, retries until `delivery.timeout.ms` (2 minutes by default) runs out, and then fails the send with a `TimeoutException`. When you see those timeouts, look for `NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS` in the warnings.

try.title: Lose a broker, then raise the bar
steps: Run the demo once with all three nodes up (command below, from the `labs` folder). It sends one payment with `acks=all` and prints where it landed.

Stop node 3 with `docker compose -f env/kafka-cluster.yml stop kafka-3`, describe the topic again (the second command of the first Try-it) and run the demo. Which ISRs changed, and which partitions got a new leader?

Every ISR still has two members. Stopping a second node would also break the controller majority, because each node here is a controller too. So raise the bar instead: `docker compose -f env/kafka-cluster.yml exec kafka-1 /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server kafka-1:19092 --alter --entity-type topics --entity-name payments --add-config min.insync.replicas=3`. Predict, then run the demo. Then run it again with `-Pargs=1` added, for `acks=1`.
Start node 3 with `docker compose -f env/kafka-cluster.yml start kafka-3`, wait a few seconds, describe the topic and run the demo once more.
Stop the cluster: `docker compose -f env/kafka-cluster.yml down -v`.

try.expect:
With three nodes up: `acks=all: written to partition 2 at offset 0` (the key `acct-17` always hashes to partition 2). After stopping node 3, broker 3 is gone from every ISR, and the partitions it led have new leaders:
```text
	Topic: payments	Partition: 0	Leader: 1	Replicas: 3,1,2	Isr: 1,2	...
	Topic: payments	Partition: 1	Leader: 1	Replicas: 1,2,3	Isr: 1,2	...
	Topic: payments	Partition: 2	Leader: 2	Replicas: 2,3,1	Isr: 1,2	...
```
The describe may first print a WARN with a stack trace saying `kafka-3` can't be resolved: the tool tried the stopped node. The demo still writes: `acks=all: written to partition 2 at offset 1`. With `min.insync.replicas=3` (trimmed):
```text
WARN ... Got error produce response with correlation id 7 on topic-partition payments-2, retrying (... attempts left). Error: NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS
... about a dozen more of these in 10 seconds ...
acks=all: refused with TimeoutException
  Expiring 1 record(s) for payments-2:10001 ms has passed since batch creation. ...
```
The leader refused every attempt, and the producer gave up at the demo's 10-second `delivery.timeout.ms`. With `-Pargs=1`: `acks=1: written to partition 2 at offset 2`. A few seconds after node 3 starts, every ISR is `1,2,3` again and the demo writes offset 3. Partition 0 stays led by broker 1 for now; the controller moves it back to its preferred leader, broker 3, on a later balance check (`leader.imbalance.check.interval.seconds`, 300). While node 3 is down the demo may also print WARN lines that `localhost:49092` can't be reached: that is the stopped node in its bootstrap list.

refs.title: Kafka 4.4 design: replication, ISR and min.insync.replicas

analogy: Think of a ledger that must be countersigned. The leader is the clerk who writes each payment into the book; the followers copy it into their own books and sign. The ISR is the list of people in the room who are keeping up, and `acks=all` means everyone in the room has signed. The high watermark is the line above which every signature is in. If people leave the room, fewer signatures are needed, down to the clerk signing alone. `min.insync.replicas` is the house rule "no payment with fewer than two signatures". The analogy breaks here: someone who left the room can return only after copying every line up to the high watermark, and the controller, not the clerk, decides who is in the room after a broker dies.
in_your_world: Your `payments` and `ledger-entries` topics should run with replication factor 3 and `min.insync.replicas=2`, and your producers with `acks=all`, the default since Kafka 3.0. Then a broker restart during a rolling deploy costs nothing, and losing two brokers at once stops writes instead of quietly keeping one copy. Your Quarkus producers will see that stop as `TimeoutException`s after `delivery.timeout.ms`, not as a clear error. So alert on partitions below their min ISR on the broker side, and make the calling code (a Temporal activity, say) treat a timed-out send as unknown: retry it with the same idempotency key rather than assuming it failed. In production, also place the three replicas in three availability zones (`broker.rack`), or one zone outage takes all three.
mistake: Believing `acks=all` alone means every acknowledged write is on three brokers. Teams set `acks=all`, leave `min.insync.replicas` at its default of 1, and assume full replication. Then one broker is slow, another is mid-restart, the ISR shrinks to the leader, and the leader keeps acknowledging writes on a single disk. If that disk dies before the followers catch up, acknowledged payments are gone. The mistake is easy because "all" sounds absolute. The fix is a topic setting, not a producer setting: replication factor 3 with `min.insync.replicas=2` on every topic that carries money.

compare.title: A durable payments producer in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java

kotlin.title: Kotlin
kotlin.src:
val producer = KafkaProducer<String, String>(
    mapOf(
        ProducerConfig.BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS_CONFIG to "localhost:29092,localhost:39092,localhost:49092",
        ProducerConfig.ACKS_CONFIG to "all",                    // wait for the whole ISR
        ProducerConfig.DELIVERY_TIMEOUT_MS_CONFIG to 120_000,   // retries of NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS end here
        ProducerConfig.KEY_SERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG to StringSerializer::class.java,
        ProducerConfig.VALUE_SERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG to StringSerializer::class.java,
    ),
)

compare.note: Kotlin passes a `mapOf(... to ...)`, which fits the producer's `Map<String, Object>` constructor; Java code often still uses `Properties`, and both work. The `ProducerConfig` constants turn a typo in a key into a compile error instead of a silently ignored setting. Notice what is missing from both: `min.insync.replicas`. It is a topic (or broker) setting, not a producer one. The producer can only ask for `acks=all`; the topic decides how many replicas that has to mean.

worked.title: Find partitions where acks=all writes are being refused

steps.say: Payments must never run on one copy. You want a check, run every minute from an ops service, that flags partitions whose ISR is below `min.insync.replicas`, which is exactly when `acks=all` producers start timing out. Start by describing the topic. (`admin` is an `Admin` client.)
Read the `min.insync.replicas` in force. It may come from the topic, the broker or the cluster, and `describeConfigs` returns whichever value applies.
steps.alt_code:
// 2. the min.insync.replicas that applies to this topic
val res = ConfigResource(ConfigResource.Type.TOPIC, "payments")
val minIsr = admin.describeConfigs(listOf(res)).all().get()
    .getValue(res).get("min.insync.replicas").value().toInt()

steps.say: Classify each partition. An ISR smaller than the replica list is under-replicated: still safe, with less margin. An ISR below `min.insync.replicas` means `acks=all` writes to that partition are being refused right now.

On the lab cluster with node 3 stopped and `min.insync.replicas=3`, every partition would land in the first branch. In production you would export these two counts as metrics rather than print them. Brokers publish the same numbers themselves (the under-replicated and under-min-ISR partition counts), and this check is the client-side version you can run from any service.

lab.title: Model the ISR and the high watermark
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder. 12 of 13 fail; the one that passes only checks the constructor you were given. Skim `ReplicatedPartitionTest`: each test is one rule from this lesson. No Docker needed.
Write `advanceHighWatermark` first: the smallest LEO among the ISR members, never lower than the current HW. Everything else calls it.

Write `append`: refuse `Acks.ALL` with `NotEnoughReplicasException` when the ISR is smaller than `minInsyncReplicas`; otherwise move the leader's LEO, advance the HW and return the last offset written.
Write `fetch`: set the follower's LEO, record the caught-up time when it reached the leader's LEO, let it rejoin the ISR once its LEO is at least the HW, then advance the HW.
Write `shrinkIsr`: remove followers that are behind the leader and have not caught up for more than `replicaLagTimeMaxMs`, then advance the HW.
Run the tests until all 13 pass. Then reread the test about the default `min.insync.replicas` of 1 and say out loud why it passes.
hints: `isr.stream().mapToLong(logEndOffset::get).min().orElseThrow()` is the smallest LEO in the ISR. Wrap it in `Math.max(highWatermark, ...)` so the HW never moves back.
In `shrinkIsr`, `isr.removeIf(...)` takes a lambda. Keep the leader out of it, and keep followers whose LEO already equals the leader's: an idle partition gives them nothing to fetch.

`NotEnoughReplicasException` is the real class from `kafka-clients` (`org.apache.kafka.common.errors`); the broker's `NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS` error becomes this exception on the client. Its constructor takes a message.

drill.title: Work out the high watermark from memory
drill.prompt: Leader 1 has LEO 120. Follower 2 has LEO 118 and is in the ISR. Follower 3 has LEO 90 and left the ISR a minute ago. `min.insync.replicas` is 2. Answer without looking: (a) what is the HW, (b) which offsets can a consumer read, (c) is an `acks=all` write accepted? Then write the HW update as one statement in Java or Kotlin, and compare.

recap: KRaft controllers keep the cluster's metadata in the `__cluster_metadata` log, replicated with Raft; a majority must agree, so run 3 or 5. ZooKeeper is gone since Kafka 4.0.
Each partition has one leader and followers that fetch from it. The ISR is the set of replicas that keep up, and the leader is always in it.
The high watermark is the smallest log end offset in the ISR. Records below it are committed, and consumers only ever see committed records.
A follower leaves the ISR when its broker is fenced (9 s without heartbeats) or when it has not caught up for `replica.lag.time.max.ms` (30 s).
`acks=all` waits for the current ISR, which can be the leader alone. `min.insync.replicas` (default 1) is the floor: use replication factor 3 with 2 for money.
Below the floor, `acks=all` writes get `NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS`, which the producer retries until `delivery.timeout.ms` and then reports as a `TimeoutException`.

quiz.q: A cluster runs 4 controllers. How many of them can fail before the metadata quorum stops accepting changes?
options: None, because an even number of controllers cannot elect a leader
quiz.why: Raft needs a majority, 3 of 4, so the quorum survives one failure: the same as 3 controllers, for one more machine. That is why controller counts are odd. Four controllers can still elect a leader, so the last option is wrong.

quiz.q: Partition 0 has ISR {1, 2, 3}. Log end offsets: leader 1 at 500, follower 2 at 500, follower 3 at 470. What is the highest offset a caught-up consumer can have read?
quiz.why: The high watermark is the smallest LEO in the ISR, 470, and consumers read only below it, so 469. Offsets 470 to 499 exist on the leader but are not committed until follower 3 has them or leaves the ISR. 499 is the tempting answer if you think consumers read the leader's log end.

quiz.q: A topic has replication factor 3 and `min.insync.replicas=2`. Two of the brokers holding `payments-0` are fenced. One producer sends with `acks=1`, another with `acks=all`. What happens?
options: Both writes are accepted, because a leader is still up
The `acks=all` write gets NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS and is retried until it times out; the `acks=1` write is accepted
The `acks=1` write is refused, and the `acks=all` write waits until the brokers return
quiz.why: `min.insync.replicas` is checked only for `acks=all`. With one replica left in the ISR, the leader refuses those writes, and the producer retries the retriable error until `delivery.timeout.ms`. An `acks=1` write needs only the leader, so it goes through, on one disk.

quiz.q: A follower's broker is alive and heartbeating, but its disk is so slow that the follower falls further and further behind. `replica.lag.time.max.ms` is the default. What do `acks=all` producers on that partition see?
options: Nothing at all: a slow follower never affects producers
Writes stall until the follower's disk recovers
Writes can stall for up to about 30 seconds, then succeed once the leader drops the slow follower from the ISR
quiz.why: While the slow follower is in the ISR it holds the high watermark back, and `acks=all` producers wait. Once it has not caught up for 30 seconds, the leader removes it, the HW moves on and the waiting writes are acknowledged. The ISR still has two members, so `min.insync.replicas=2` is met and nothing is refused.

quiz.q: From lesson 1: the leader of `payments-0` has log end offset 1,250, but a slow follower holds the high watermark at 1,200. A consumer group has committed offset 1,000. Which statement is right?
options: The group can read up to offset 1,249 right now
The group can read offsets 1,000 to 1,199; the rest become readable once they are committed
The group cannot read anything until the follower catches up
The group's committed offset jumps to 1,200 on its own
quiz.why: A consumer reads only committed records, those below the high watermark, so the end of the partition as consumers see it is 1,200, and lag is measured against that. Offsets 1,200 to 1,249 appear as soon as the ISR has them. A committed offset moves only when the group commits.

flashcards.front: What do KRaft controllers store, and where?
flashcards.back: The cluster metadata (live brokers, topics, partition leaders, ISRs) as records in the one-partition `__cluster_metadata` log, replicated with Raft.
A partition's in-sync replicas: the leader plus the followers that have reached the leader's end within `replica.lag.time.max.ms` (30 s by default).
The smallest log end offset in the ISR. Records below it are committed and visible to consumers.
Every replica currently in the ISR. If the ISR is only the leader, the leader alone.
Sets the smallest ISR size at which the leader accepts `acks=all` writes; below it they get NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS. The default is 1.

flashcards.front: How does a producer handle NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS?
flashcards.back: It is retriable: the producer retries until `delivery.timeout.ms` (2 minutes) runs out, then fails the send with a TimeoutException.

flashcards.front: What is an unclean leader election?
flashcards.back: Making a replica outside the ISR the leader. It can lose committed records, so it is off by default (`unclean.leader.election.enable=false`).

terms.plain: Kafka's built-in Raft protocol for storing cluster metadata. The only mode since Kafka 4.0, which removed ZooKeeper.
A node that keeps the cluster metadata. One controller is active (the Raft leader); a majority must agree on each change.
A broker the controller no longer treats as alive, usually after 9 seconds without heartbeats. It loses its leaderships and ISR places.
How many brokers hold a copy of each partition of a topic.
The leader replica takes all reads and writes for a partition; followers fetch from it to keep their copies current.
In-sync replicas: the leader plus the followers that keep up with it.
The smallest log end offset in the ISR. Records below it are committed.
The smallest ISR size at which a partition accepts `acks=all` writes.

explain_back.prompt: Your team lead asks: "We use acks=all, so every acknowledged payment is on three brokers, right?" Explain what acks=all really guarantees, and what you would change.
explain_back.answer: Not quite. `acks=all` makes the leader wait until every replica currently in the ISR has the record, and the ISR shrinks whenever a follower hasn't caught up for 30 seconds or its broker is fenced. If the ISR is down to the leader, `acks=all` is satisfied by one copy on one disk, and with the default `min.insync.replicas` of 1 the leader accepts that. I'd set `min.insync.replicas=2` on the payments topics, with replication factor 3. Then every acknowledged write is on at least two brokers, and when only one in-sync replica is left the leader refuses `acks=all` writes instead of pretending. We'd also alert on partitions below their min ISR, because producers only see those refusals as timeouts.

deeper.body:
Kafka 4.0 shipped the first part of KIP-966, **eligible leader replicas** (ELR), and since 4.1 it is on by default for new clusters. The lab cluster has it: `kafka-features.sh --bootstrap-server kafka-1:19092 describe` lists `eligible.leader.replicas.version` at level 1.

ELR closes a gap in the rules above. Suppose the ISR shrinks below `min.insync.replicas`, the leader stops accepting `acks=all` writes, and then the leader dies. Picking only from the ISR may leave no candidate at all, and an unclean election would lose data. With ELR the controller remembers replicas that left the ISR while it was below `min.insync.replicas` and that still hold every committed record, and it can elect one of them safely. ELR also makes the high watermark stop advancing while the ISR is below `min.insync.replicas`, so the setting really becomes the minimum number of copies of every committed record. Jack Vanlightly checked the design with a TLA+ model (see Sources).

You can see it on the lab cluster. With `min.insync.replicas=3` on `payments`, pausing broker 2 for about half a minute (`docker compose -f env/kafka-cluster.yml pause kafka-2`, then `unpause`) made `kafka-topics.sh --describe` show `Isr: 1,3` and `Elr: 2`: broker 2 had left the ISR but stayed a safe candidate. The describe command itself can hang for up to 30 seconds while a broker is paused.

Two rules from the ELR docs: once ELR is on, set `min.insync.replicas` at the cluster level rather than per broker, and changing it clears the ELR state.
